title: Inflation Targeting in India after 2016: Policy Credibility versus Structural Constraints
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Inflation Targeting in India after 2016: Policy Credibility versus Structural Constraints
detail.abstract: India's adoption of a flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework in 2016 marked a significant transformation in its macroeconomic policy regime. By formally assigning the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) the mandate of maintaining Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation at 4 percent within a tolerance band of ±2 percent, the framework aimed to enhance policy credibility and anchor inflation expectations. This paper examines inflation dynamics in India during the postadoption period (2016-2024), with particular emphasis on the interaction between monetary policy, supply-side factors, and global shocks. Using secondary data from official sources and a descriptive macroeconomic analytical approach, the study evaluates the effectiveness and limitations of inflation targeting in a developing economy context. The analysis finds that while the framework improved transparency and expectations management, headline inflation outcomes remained highly sensitive to supply-side disturbances. The paper argues that inflation targeting in India functions more as an expectations-anchoring mechanism than a direct inflation control tool, highlighting the need for coordinated monetary, fiscal, and structural policy interventions.

title: The Jurisdictional Architecture of International Commercial Arbitration: A Comprehensive Analysis of Competence-Competence and Judicial Oversight
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: The Jurisdictional Architecture of International Commercial Arbitration: A Comprehensive Analysis of Competence-Competence and Judicial Oversight
detail.abstract: The functional integrity of international commercial arbitration as an autonomous dispute resolution mechanism is fundamentally anchored in the principles of competence-competence and the doctrine of separability. This report provides an exhaustive examination of the legal frameworks governing the allocation of jurisdictional authority between arbitral tribunals and national courts. Beginning with the historical genesis of the "who decides" rule in the landmark Prima Paint decision, the analysis explores the systematic codification of these principles within Article 16 of the UNCITRAL Model Law. Central to this discussion is the distinction between the positive and negative effects of competence-competence, with a particular focus on the legitimacy effects articulated by Professor Bernard Hanotiau and the nuanced differentiation between jurisdiction and admissibility. The report further investigates modern judicial standards of review, contrasting the prima facie approach established in the Singaporean Firstlink and Tomolugen jurisprudence against more interventionist regimes. Furthermore, it addresses the complex interaction between the Brussels I Recast Regulation and the arbitration exception, the challenges of multi-contract coverage under the Fiona Trust presumption, and contemporary practitioner insights from the 2024 Queen Mary University of London (QMUL) International Arbitration Survey. Through this multi-dimensional analysis, the report elucidates the evolving balance between party autonomy and the rule of law in the global arbitral landscape.

detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations operate under conditions of persistent uncertainty, competing priorities, and structural contradictions. Although existing leadership theories acknowledge organizational tension, they largely conceptualize it as a condition to be minimized or resolved. This paper proposes the Tension-Adaptive-Contextual Leadership (TACL) Theory, a standalone conceptual framework that reconceptualizes tension as a deliberate and productive design variable of managerial leadership. The TACL model explains how effective leaders intentionally generate, regulate, and utilize organizational tension to enable adaptation and coordinated action. The framework is structured around three interdependent leadership mechanisms: strategic tension creation, through which leaders sustain productive imbalance between competing demands; adaptive sense-making, which translates tension into shared understanding and direction; and contextual authority shifting, whereby decision-making authority dynamically moves between centralized and distributed forms in response to situational demands. By formalizing tension as a core analytical construct and specifying clear causal mechanisms, the TACL theory advances leadership scholarship beyond equilibrium-oriented models. The paper articulates a set of theoretical propositions to support future empirical testing and positions the framework as particularly relevant for volatile, resource-constrained, and non-routine organizational contexts. Overall, the TACL model offers a new lens for understanding managerial leadership effectiveness in environments where tension is unavoidable and equilibrium is neither achievable nor desirable.

detail.abstract: This conceptual case analysis examines the public confrontation between Ryanair and Elon Musk as an example of deliberate brand provocation executed under conditions of asymmetric attention. Rather than interpreting the exchange as reactive corporate behavior, the paper frames Ryanair's response as a strategically governed communication act embedded within its long-standing brand architecture. Drawing on theories of brand salience, earned media efficiency, corporate brand voice governance, and archetypal consistency, the analysis evaluates both the value creation and latent risks associated with antagonistic brand behavior. The case demonstrates how provocation, when archetypically coherent and commercially anchored, can enhance mental availability and convert attention into transactional outcomes without eroding strategic legitimacy. The paper contributes to marketing scholarship by clarifying the boundary conditions under which corporate brands can engage high-profile individuals in public discourse while maintaining governance discipline and category credibility. Implications are discussed for brand strategists, senior executives, and scholars examining executive communication in attention-driven markets.

title: Forecasting Correctional Facility Bed Demand Using Autoregressive and Neural Network Models: An Empirical Analysis of 154,337 Admissions with Cross-Domain Validation

detail.title: Forecasting Correctional Facility Bed Demand Using Autoregressive and Neural Network Models: An Empirical Analysis of 154,337 Admissions with Cross-Domain Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required. This study uses aggregate administrative data with no individual identifiers.

detail.abstract: Available beds in correctional facilities tend to fill regardless of facility size, yet there is no correlation between crime rates and incarceration rates—bed demand is driven by often unexamined policies across the criminal justice system's adjudication decision points. Despite the critical importance of demand forecasting for infrastructure investment and operations, empirical studies applying modern statistical and machine learning methods to large-scale correctional administrative data remain scarce. This paper addresses this gap through four contributions. First, we present an empirical analysis of 154,337 individual admission-release records spanning 10 provincial correctional facilities in Alberta, Canada (April 2015–August 2020), characterizing admission dynamics (32.7% decline from 2016 to 2019), length-of-stay distributions (mean 47.2 days, median 14 days), and facility-level heterogeneity across remand centres (mean LOS 38–49 days) and correctional centres (mean LOS 95–97 days). Second, we quantify the impact of COVID-19 with facility-level granularity, documenting a 38.3% collapse in admissions and a 27.0–31.6% reduction in provincial custody populations. Third, we develop and compare multiple forecasting approaches—including stepwise autoregressive models and neural network architectures—achieving a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 2.18% on the total custody population model across 63 months of validation, with disaggregated 24-month ahead forecasts for sentenced and unsentenced populations including 95% confidence intervals. Fourth, we validate cross-domain generalizability by applying the same automated forecasting framework to criminal, civil, and family court caseloads using socioeconomic covariates (unemployment rate, income distribution). The analysis draws on structural parallels between correctional and clinical inpatient facility dynamics to motivate the transfer of healthcare operations research methods—including stochastic patient-flow models and nonlinear autoregressive neural networks (NARX)—to correctional capacity planning. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to combine individual-level correctional admission data at this scale with automated model comparison, cross-domain validation, and COVID-19 impact quantification in a Canadian provincial context.

affiliations: University of Virginia (UVA) School of Law - Alumni/Adjunct/Student

detail.title: Rate Your Experience: Comparative Lessons for Gig Work

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Journal of Tax Law, Volume 18, Fall 2026

detail.abstract:
What happens when millions of workers earn their livelihoods through platforms designed to avoid the legal and fiscal responsibilities of traditional employment? This Article argues that the answer turns not primarily on how those workers are classified, but on whether platform earnings are institutionally designed to generate social insurance entitlements. Across jurisdictions, gig worker precarity persists where income fails to attach automatically to health coverage, retirement security, and income replacement, even when workers are formally eligible for protection.

Existing U.S. scholarship has done important work diagnosing compliance gaps and proposing reforms to lower reporting thresholds, expand withholding, and improve taxpayer education. But this literature largely stops at the point where platform earnings become visible to the state, treating revenue collection as an end rather than a means. This is a mistake: visibility without integration does nothing to guarantee that gig workers accrue health insurance, Social Security credits, or unemployment benefits. In short, we have been asking the wrong question focusing on classification fights and revenue loss while neglecting the architecture that determines whether earnings become entitlements.

Drawing on a comparative analysis of Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, France, and Germany, this Article reframes the debate over platform work by shifting attention from classification to benefit attachment. It shows that jurisdictions are increasingly moving away from protracted status disputes toward presumptions of employment, not as symbolic reclassification, but as institutional mechanisms to secure automatic, mandatory contributions to social insurance. Where participation is voluntary or opt-in, coverage remains fragmented; where contribution and collection mechanisms are integrated, protection attaches to gig work even outside standard employment. The Article concludes with design lessons for U.S. policymakers: delinking social protection from a single-employer model, mandating portable coverage, and using tax infrastructure as the gatekeeper through which platform earnings become social entitlements.

title: Conceptual Aspects of the Functioning of an Independent Music Label in the Context of the Digital Transformation of the Global Media Space, Using the ATTRA_048 Ecosystem as an Example

detail.abstract:
The digital transformation of the music industry has been one of the most significant phenomena of recent decades, radically changing the ways in which music content is created, distributed, and consumed. From the advent of PCs and MIDI technology to the widespread adoption of streaming services and social platforms, digital technologies have transformed the economics and culture of music, creating new opportunities for artists and, at the same time, significant challenges for traditional industry models. 

On the one hand, the internet and streaming platforms have significantly lowered barriers to entry for musicians and independent projects, allowing them to create, publish, and promote music without the need for support from mainstream corporations. On the other hand, this has led to the emergence of new competitive formats, where algorithmic recommendation systems and consumer behavior data shape the visibility and commercial success of content. 

These digital shifts have affected not only the technical side of music production, but also the structure of the market, strengthening the role of independent artists and labels in the global media space. It is in such conditions that autonomous music ecosystems are formed, capable of functioning without the traditional intermediation of large music corporations. [3]

Digital transformation is not a temporary stage in the development of the music industry but rather shapes a new structural norm for its functioning. In this context, independent music labels are no longer marginal market players but are becoming full-fledged actors in the digital cultural economy, capable of competing with traditional industrial models not through capital but through flexibility, speed of adaptation, and strategic use of digital tools.

title: Human-AI Collaboration Models in Organizational Decision-Making

detail.title: Human-AI Collaboration Models in Organizational Decision-Making
detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational decision-making has transformed how businesses analyze data, forecast trends, and allocate resources. This study explores human-AI collaboration models, focusing on the interplay between human expertise and AI-driven insights in decision processes. It categorizes collaboration frameworks into three primary models: AI-assisted, AI-augmented, and AI-autonomous decision-making, highlighting their respective roles in enhancing accuracy, efficiency, and strategic alignment. The research examines factors influencing effective collaboration, including trust, interpretability, cognitive workload, and organizational culture. Case studies from finance, healthcare, and supply chain management illustrate practical applications and outcomes of these models. Findings suggest that optimal decision-making emerges from a balanced integration of human judgment and AI capabilities, emphasizing the importance of adaptive collaboration strategies. This study contributes to organizational theory by providing a framework for deploying AI in decision-making while maintaining human oversight and accountability.

title: Talent Management and Recruitment Automation

detail.title: Talent Management and Recruitment Automation
detail.abstract: The accelerating adoption of digital technologies has fundamentally reshaped organizational approaches to talent management and recruitment. In response to increasingly competitive labor markets, skill shortages, and the demand for faster, more objective hiring decisions, organizations are progressively integrating automation and artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment and talent management processes. This study examines the conceptual foundations, technological architectures, and organizational implications of recruitment automation within the broader framework of talent management. Drawing on an extensive synthesis of contemporary academic literature and industry practices, the paper analyzes how automated systems influence candidate sourcing, screening, assessment, selection, and long-term workforce planning. Particular attention is paid to algorithmic decision-making, data-driven talent analytics, and the integration of human judgment with automated tools. The findings indicate that recruitment automation enhances efficiency, scalability, and consistency in hiring outcomes, while simultaneously introducing challenges related to algorithmic bias, transparency, data governance, and ethical accountability. The study concludes that recruitment automation should not be conceptualized as a replacement for human expertise, but rather as a socio-technical system that requires careful governance, continuous evaluation, and strategic alignment with organizational values. This paper contributes to the growing body of research on digital human resource management by offering an integrative framework that situates recruitment automation as a core pillar of contemporary talent management strategy.

detail.title: Predictive Analytics and Machine Learning for Strategic Business
detail.abstract: Predictive analytics and machine learning have become central to strategic business intelligence by enabling organizations to transform large volumes of structured and unstructured data into actionable insights. This study examines how machine learning techniques enhance predictive analytics capabilities to support data-driven strategic decision-making in modern enterprises. The paper reviews key machine learning models used in business intelligence, including regression methods, decision trees, ensemble learning, and neural networks, and evaluates their effectiveness in forecasting market trends, customer behavior, financial performance, and operational risks. It further explores the integration of predictive analytics within business intelligence systems, highlighting how real-time analytics, automation, and advanced data visualization improve managerial insight and organizational agility. Challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, ethical considerations, and organizational readiness are also discussed. The study concludes that the strategic adoption of predictive analytics and machine learning significantly enhances competitive advantage by improving forecast accuracy, optimizing resource allocation, and enabling proactive decision-making. The findings provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to align advanced analytics with long-term business strategy and identify directions for future research in intelligent decision support systems.

title: Explainable AI (XAI) in Enterprise Decision Support Systems

detail.title: Explainable AI (XAI) in Enterprise Decision Support Systems
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in enterprise decision support systems has transformed organizational decision-making by enabling data-driven insights and predictive analytics. However, the opacity of many AI models, particularly complex machine learning algorithms, poses challenges in trust, accountability, and regulatory compliance. Explainable AI (XAI) addresses these challenges by providing transparency into AI decision processes, allowing stakeholders to understand, validate, and act upon model outputs confidently. This paper explores the integration of XAI in enterprise decision support systems, examining techniques for interpretability, model-agnostic versus model-specific approaches, and the impact of explainability on decision quality, user trust, and organizational performance. Through a review of current methodologies and case studies, the study highlights best practices for implementing XAI frameworks in business environments and outlines future research directions for enhancing human-AI collaboration in strategic decision-making.

title: Data-Driven Talent Analytics and Skills Intelligence Platforms

detail.title: Data-Driven Talent Analytics and Skills Intelligence Platforms
detail.abstract: The rapid pace of digital transformation, automation, and artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping workforce requirements across industries. Organizations increasingly face critical skills gaps, talent shortages, and misalignment between existing workforce capabilities and future strategic needs. Data-driven talent analytics and skills intelligence platforms have emerged as powerful solutions to address these challenges by leveraging large-scale workforce data, machine learning, and advanced analytics to inform evidence-based talent decisions. This study examines the architecture, capabilities, and organizational impact of data-driven talent analytics and skills intelligence platforms. It synthesizes current research and industry practices to explore how these platforms integrate heterogeneous data sources-including human resource information systems, learning management systems, labor market data, and employee-generated signals-to generate real-time insights into skills demand, supply, proficiency, and adjacency. Key applications analyzed include workforce planning, skills gap analysis, internal mobility, personalized learning pathways, and strategic reskilling initiatives. The findings indicate that organizations adopting skills intelligence platforms achieve improved talent visibility, more accurate workforce forecasting, enhanced diversity and inclusion outcomes, and greater agility in responding to market disruptions. However, challenges related to data quality, algorithmic bias, privacy, and organizational adoption remain significant barriers. The study concludes that data-driven talent analytics is transitioning from a supportive HR function to a core strategic capability. Skills intelligence platforms are becoming essential infrastructure for future-ready organizations, enabling continuous workforce adaptation, evidence-based decision-making, and sustainable competitive advantage in the evolving digital economy.

title: Decision Intelligence and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)

detail.title: Decision Intelligence and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)
detail.abstract: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems have long served as the transactional backbone of modern organizations, integrating core business functions such as finance, operations, supply chain, and human resources into unified digital platforms. However, while ERP systems excel at data standardization and process automation, they have historically fallen short in supporting complex, adaptive, and forward-looking decision-making. In parallel, Decision Intelligence (DI) has emerged as an interdisciplinary paradigm that combines data analytics, artificial intelligence, decision theory, and domain knowledge to systematically improve organizational decisions. This study examines the conceptual and practical integration of Decision Intelligence within ERP ecosystems, positioning DI as a critical evolution beyond traditional business intelligence and reporting layers. Through a structured analytical synthesis of existing literature, system architectures, and organizational use cases, the paper develops a comprehensive framework that explains how DI augments ERP systems by embedding predictive, prescriptive, and cognitive decision capabilities directly into enterprise workflows. The findings demonstrate that DI-enabled ERP systems enhance decision quality, organizational agility, and strategic alignment, while also introducing new challenges related to data governance, model transparency, and human-AI collaboration. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions and managerial implications for enterprises seeking to transition from transaction-centric ERP systems to intelligence-driven decision platforms.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven decision intelligence systems are increasingly embedded in critical organizational and societal decision-making processes, ranging from healthcare diagnostics and financial risk assessment to public policy design and supply-chain optimization. While these systems promise enhanced efficiency, predictive accuracy, and scalability, their growing autonomy and opacity raise profound ethical and governance challenges. This paper critically examines the ethical risks and governance gaps associated with AI-based decision intelligence systems, focusing on issues of transparency, accountability, bias, autonomy, and institutional oversight. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature from AI ethics, governance studies, and socio-technical systems theory, the study synthesizes existing knowledge to identify structural weaknesses in current governance approaches. The analysis reveals that prevailing regulatory and organizational frameworks remain reactive, fragmented, and insufficiently aligned with the dynamic, learning-based nature of modern AI systems. The paper argues that effective governance of decision intelligence requires a shift from compliance-oriented controls toward adaptive, value-embedded, and lifecycle-based governance models. By articulating a comprehensive conceptual framework for ethical AI governance, this study contributes to ongoing debates on responsible AI deployment and provides actionable insights for policymakers, system designers, and organizational leaders seeking to balance innovation with societal trust.

detail.abstract: The growing complexity of enterprise environments, characterized by large-scale data heterogeneity, uncertainty, and rapid market dynamics, has exposed the limitations of traditional rule-based and deterministic decision support systems. Cognitive computing has emerged as a transformative paradigm that integrates artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, and knowledge representation to emulate human-like reasoning in organizational decision-making. This study examines the role of cognitive computing in enhancing enterprise decision support systems (EDSS), with particular emphasis on adaptive learning, contextual awareness, and explainability. Through a conceptual and analytical synthesis of recent enterprise deployments and cognitive architectures, the paper demonstrates how cognitive decision support systems enable organizations to transition from reactive decision-making toward predictive and prescriptive intelligence. The findings indicate that cognitive computing significantly improves decision quality, operational agility, and strategic alignment by enabling continuous learning from structured and unstructured data sources. However, the study also identifies critical challenges related to trust, transparency, data governance, and organizational readiness that constrain large-scale adoption. The paper concludes by proposing a research-informed framework for integrating cognitive computing into enterprise decision ecosystems, emphasizing human-AI collaboration, ethical governance, and scalable system design.

detail.abstract: This white paper examines a class of systemic risk emerging from the convergence of advanced artificial intelligence and increasingly accessible quantum computing capabilities. Rather than focusing on speculative futures such as artificial general intelligence or total cryptographic collapse, it analyzes how incremental progress, uneven access, and large-scale deployment interact to produce destabilizing effects. Artificial intelligence functions as a force multiplier that accelerates decision-making and amplifies intent, while quantum computing introduces selective, asymmetric advantage. Together, these dynamics create interaction effects that existing governance and risk frameworks are poorly equipped to recognize. The resulting risks accumulate below formal thresholds, manifest through erosion rather than sudden failure, and can extend from institutions to national stability itself. The paper is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, arguing that effective response depends first on institutional recognition of convergence risk as a distinct and immediate challenge.

title: What Language tells us about the Indian Investor
affiliations: and Finance, IIM Nagpur, MIHAN, Nagpur

detail.title: What Language tells us about the Indian Investor
detail.abstract: This study documents how cultural differences proxied through language singularly explains investor behaviours and risk preferences beyond demographic and socioeconomic characteristics. Language as a cultural aggregator with risk, trust, ambiguity as predictors of investing and risk-taking was employed in a mixed multi-level model. Risk perception (low) and specific trust (high) related to investing varied significantly amongst language groups and explained why some groups invested significantly more despite similar socioeconomic and demographic profiles. Ambiguity intolerance a measure of individual uncertainty showed no significant variation across cultural groupings and had no effect on investing preferences. Risk aversion a general measure of risk did not vary significantly across cultural groups and as expected had a negative effect on risk-taking preferences but no effect on degree of investing. Migrants defined as those who spoke a language not native to the region showed greater risktaking preferences due to lower risk aversion. These results are robust to a variety of demographic and socioeconomic factors. Investors in mutual funds are influenced more by risk perception and trust levels learnt through a common cultural grouping than by their individual risk aversion and tolerance for ambiguity. Risk taking on the other hand is guided by individual risk aversion and economic factors. This subtle difference suggests focus should be more on language groupings or other cultural markers to enhance adoption and penetration of investing behaviors rather than rely solely on assessing individual and socioeconomic attributes.

title: Candidate Behavior in Local Elections: Campaigning in the Digital Age

detail.title: Candidate Behavior in Local Elections: Campaigning in the Digital Age

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by CAPES.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how electoral institutions shape candidates' digital campaign strategies, exploiting Brazil's 200,000-voter runoff threshold in a regression discontinuity design. We combine official campaign finance records from the 2024 municipal elections with highfrequency Instagram advertising data from Meta's Marketing API-57,677 ads matched to 540 candidates. We document three patterns of digital campaigning: near-instantaneous ad deployment, a strong preference for broad demographic reach over micro-targeting, and a sharp escalation in advertising intensity as election day approaches. Runoff-eligible candidates reduce their digital boosting budget share by approximately 4 p.p in the first round, with the effect concentrated in the final weeks and driven entirely by competitive candidates. No other expenditure category responds to the threshold. This strategic reallocation operates through scale rather than content: candidates above the threshold accumulate approximately 866,000 fewer impressions without altering the format, duration, or cost structure of individual ads. Consistent with this timing behavior, we find that an increase of BRL 100,000 in digital boosting is associated with a 5 p.p increase in vote share, with total reach-not content-driving electoral returns. These findings reveal digital advertising as a strategically flexible instrument whose near-zero marginal deployment cost enables intertemporal allocation decisions that traditional media cannot accommodate.

detail.title: Inclusive Tourism in a Plural India
detail.abstract: India's tourism sector is uniquely positioned at the intersection of cultural plurality, economic development, and sustainability imperatives. As one of the most culturally diverse nations in the world, India presents both opportunities and challenges in leveraging tourism as a vehicle for inclusive growth and sustainable development. This conceptual paper explores how inclusive and sustainable tourism can function as a catalyst for cultural integration and economic inclusion, particularly among marginalized communities such as rural populations, indigenous groups, women entrepreneurs, and informal sector workers. Drawing upon theories of inclusive growth, sustainable development, stakeholder participation, and cultural economy, the study proposes a conceptual framework linking tourism development with social equity, cultural preservation, and local economic empowerment. The paper critically examines contemporary tourism practices in India, highlighting gaps between policy intent and grassroots implementation, while emphasizing the need for community-centered, environmentally responsible, and culturally sensitive tourism models. By synthesizing existing literature and policy perspectives, the paper contributes to tourism scholarship by positioning inclusive and sustainable tourism not merely as a sectoral strategy, but as an integrative development paradigm aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The study offers theoretical insights and policy directions for reimagining India's tourism future through the lens of pluralism, sustainability, and shared prosperity.

title: Exchange of Crypto Information in the ‘Pre-AEOI Phase’: Can Non-CARF Countries Use Group Requests To Obtain Information From Foreign CASPs?

detail.title: Exchange of Crypto Information in the ‘Pre-AEOI Phase’: Can Non-CARF Countries Use Group Requests To Obtain Information From Foreign CASPs?

keywords: request for the exchange of information

detail.abstract:
The article examines the use of "group requests" by countries to obtain information on crypto assets held by their residents through foreign Crypto Asset Service Providers (CASPs). With information exchanged under the OECD’s Crypto Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) set to commence in 2027, many Global South nations remain uncommitted due to administrative constraint. Many of these countries host significant domestic crypto markets. The author proposes that group requests can serve as a powerful alternative to "mimic" the compliance effects of automatic exchange of information under the CARF.

The study outlines a practical methodology for executing these requests. It begins by identifying how countries can overcome the lack of comprehensive macroeconomic data on cross border crypto activities. Countries can use the methodology developed by  the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) methodology to identify relevant CASP jurisdictions. It then details the conditions for validity under the OECD’s "foreseeable relevance" standard, ensuring requests are not dismissed as illegal "fishing expeditions". Finally, the article analyzes the legal viability of basing such requests on bilateral tax treaties, tax information exchange agreements (TIEAs), and the Multilateral Convention (MAAC). The article concludes by providing a checklist for a successful use by tax authorities of crypto group requests.

detail.abstract: This work presents a comprehensive study of the mechanisms of integration of independent artists into the global music ecosystem. The author justifies the transition from a model of spontaneous popularity to strategic engineering of social connections, where the synergy of academic qualifications, institutional membership, and algorithmic collaborations plays a key role. The work analyzes the importance of professional associations (NATS, HipHopAlliance, ISSA) as tools for creating a “reputation shield” that allows artists to minimize investment risks and gain access to closed industry resources. Particular attention is paid to the scientific verification of creative activity through publications in academic repositories (SSRN), which transforms a personal brand into the status of an intellectual expert. A practical algorithm has been developed for establishing direct contacts with top American artists (using the examples of OG Maco and Mytee Dee) based on the theory of network centrality and the concept of “fan trading.” The manual contains step-by-step recommendations for the legal and technical implementation of joint projects, the integration of Web3 technologies, and the optimization of digital distribution. The publication is aimed at music entrepreneurs, independent performers, and cultural industry managers who seek to scale local success to the level of sustainable international authority.

title: Project Fleet 1715: Axiomatic Numerical Synthesis and Absolute Point of Certainty
affiliations: Founder, Unified Principle

detail.title: Project Fleet 1715: Axiomatic Numerical Synthesis and Absolute Point of Certainty
detail.abstract: The 1715 Spanish Treasure Fleet, lost off the Florida coast during the catastrophic hurricane of July 31, 1715, has been the subject of centuries of salvage attempts. Traditional recovery strategies rely on probabilistic drift modeling, magnetic anomaly detection, and reactive search technologies. These methods are inherently limited by their reliance on incomplete historical data, stochastic modeling assumptions, and environmental variance. This paper presents a fully deterministic, hyper-axiomatic approach to locating the maximal remaining concentration of the fleet's un-recovered primary contraband cargo, using a methodology we term the Unified Principle. The Unified Principle integrates 14 hyper-deterministic force vectors (Yang) with high-resolution terrain traps (Yin), cross-referenced against three centuries of recovered cargo data (Presence) and the undrawn inventory deficit (Absence). Utilizing a 56-point geodetic grid framework and the 364-Day Axiom for temporal phase-locking, the methodology collapses all variables into a single pre-verified coordinate of absolute certainty: 27.842718 N,-80.481903 W (WGS84). This paper details the complete numerical synthesis, differential void analysis, terrain modeling, vector integration, and geodetic computation underlying this result. The methodology is fully self-contained, providing explicit mathematical, historical, and geospatial data sufficient for SSRN peer review. Appendices describe inventory tables, vector magnitudes, bathymetric analyses, and phase-locking calculations. The Unified Principle demonstrates a novel approach to deterministic modeling in historical maritime recovery, establishing a replicable, operational-ready framework that eliminates the need for probabilistic search.

detail.abstract: Housing First (HF) critics argue that Treatment First (TF) reduces moral hazard, which discourages drug use, strengthens labor-market attachment, and lowers homelessness. Supporters counter that TF increases homelessness and addiction because recovery is harder while homeless. A general-equilibrium model links homelessness, drug use, addiction, mortality, and labor-market outcomes. Individuals trade off the immediate utility of drugs against the expected loss in future life value from higher mortality risk. Unlike existing approaches, the model generates drug use concentrated among low-income individuals without assuming preference heterogeneity. Relative to rationed HF, TF with no rationing reduces addiction and homelessness and is nearly self-financing.

title: Wealth Composition and Stock Market Participation: Evidence from a Correlated Random Effects Model

detail.title: Wealth Composition and Stock Market Participation: Evidence from a Correlated Random Effects Model
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the gap between portfolio choice theory and observed household behavior by examining how wealth composition influences stock market participation. I develop a participation model where illiquid real assets generate background risk, increasing effective risk aversion under Risk Vulnerability. Empirically, I exploit the panel structure of the Bank of Italy's Survey on Household Income and Wealth (2006-2022) to test the model's implications through a Correlated Random Effects Probit framework. This methodological approach allows for isolating the effect of wealth composition from unobserved time-invariant household heterogeneity. The results confirm that, conditional on total net wealth and financial human capital, larger holdings of real estate and business equity significantly reduce the probability of stock market participation. I document that this crowding-out effect intensifies at higher wealth levels. This empirical pattern challenges purely liquidity-based explanations and supports the hypothesis that background risk from illiquid assets is a structural determinant of the limited participation phenomenon.

Leveraging the Unified Principle (UP), this architecture formalizes system autonomy as the conservation of internal coherence under bounded perception and finite state resolution. By combining Photo-Kinetic Harvesting Surfaces (P-KHS), Aero-Kinetic Recovery (A-KR) Ducts, and Integrated Energy Orchestration (IEO), the system maximizes environmental energy extraction and operational autonomy. title: Demand Elasticity in the Primary Market for Corporate Bonds

detail.title: Demand Elasticity in the Primary Market for Corporate Bonds
detail.abstract: In this paper, we establish the role of primary market investor demand elasticity as a key driver of corporate bond issuance costs and underwriter pricing decisions. We introduce a model-free bond-level measure of demand elasticity using novel bookbuilding data from which we observe two pairs of prices and quantity along the offering day demand curve. We demonstrate the time series and cross-sectional characteristics of demand elasticity, which varies systematically with credit quality, maturity, and market conditions, and declines during periods of market stress. Higher demand elasticity is associated with lower underpricing, offering spreads, and order book sizes, and is related to characteristics of investors participating in the primary market. Our estimates also provide a useful comparison to those using structural models and demand shocks to explain demand elasticity based on secondary market prices.

title: Forecasting and Managing Volatility with Machine Learning

detail.title: Forecasting and Managing Volatility with Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Using intraday S&P 500 data from 1998 to 2023, we examine the performance of machine learning (ML)-based volatility forecasts. We construct two predictor sets to isolate two key differences of ML methods relative to widely used heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark models: their potential for learning more complex functional forms from the same predictors, and their ability to accommodate a more granular predictor set. Our findings indicate that linear ML models perform similarly to HAR models in out-of-sample forecasting. Among nonlinear ML models, gradient-boosted trees improve predictive performance, whereas results for neural networks are mixed. Notably, ML models trained on the granular predictor set typically perform worse. We also observe that nonlinear ML models exhibit greater performance dispersion across volatility levels. Finally, we evaluate whether ML-based forecasts improve volatility control when applied to target volatility strategies. While simple forecasts achieve substantial reduction in the volatility of volatility compared to static allocations, the incremental gains of ML methods are modest at best.

title: The Solar Paradox: Pure Social Diffusion and Competitive Resource Capture in Semi-Arid Irrigated Land Expansion
affiliations: , University of Jendouba, Sousse University and Datadoit

detail.title: The Solar Paradox: Pure Social Diffusion and Competitive Resource Capture in Semi-Arid Irrigated Land Expansion
detail.abstract: Solar-powered irrigation is expanding rapidly across semi-arid regions, but the mechanisms through which this technology diffuses in informal groundwater economies-where the majority of wells operate without permits-remain poorly understood. We address this gap through a spatiotemporal analysis of 3,201 solar wells identified via satellite census in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, combined with 10,000 control points. Cox proportional hazards models reveal that terrain accessibility is the dominant spatial determinant: slope reduces the adoption hazard by 66% (HR = 0.339, p < 0.001), with proximity to urban centers (HR = 0.700) and lower elevation (HR = 0.718) also significant. Bass diffusion model estimation yields a near-zero innovation coefficient (p = 0.001) alongside a high imitation coefficient (q = 0.679)-the first documented case of p ≈ 0 in agricultural technology diffusion, indicating a complete absence of institutional influence over the adoption process. We attribute this to a multi-layer governance failure in which legal barriers, financial exclusion, and extension collapse block all formal technology transfer channels. A neighbor effects model reveals that higher local adopter density slows subsequent adoption (HR = 0.606, p < 0.001), creating an apparent paradox with the high aggregate imitation. We reconcile this through a Competitive Diffusion Framework distinguishing an aggregate-level Information Effect from a local-level Congestion Effect linked to aquifer stress. The Finance Law 2025's pivot to retroactive regularization of unauthorized wells confirms that informal diffusion has outpaced regulatory capacity, marking a transition from administrative exclusion to fiscal capture in Tunisia's groundwater governance.

title: Output, Value added and Import Multipliers in an Interregional Input – Output Model: Evidence from Mekong Delta and Rest of Vietnam (ROV)

detail.title: Output, Value added and Import Multipliers in an Interregional Input – Output Model: Evidence from Mekong Delta and Rest of Vietnam (ROV)
detail.abstract:
This study estimates and compares output, value added and import multipliers within an interregional input-output (IRIO) framework for the Mekong Delta and the Rest of Vietnam (ROV). Using the most recent interregional IO table constructed for Vietnam (2024), the paper quantifies how regional production structures, trade linkages, and sourcing patterns shape the dependence on domestic and foreign imports. The analysis decomposes total import multipliers into intra multiplier, interregional feedback loops and interregional spillover effects, allowing us to identify the channels through which each region transmits import demand to the rest of the economy.
The study contributes to the literature by providing the first empirical evidence on output, value added and import multipliers in a two-region IRIO setting for Vietnam. The findings offer policy insights for regional integration, supply-chain stability, and strategies to reduce import dependence in key sectors of the Mekong Delta.

title: Do Exporting Manufacturing Plants Invest Relatively More in Pollution Control Equipment than Non-Exporting Plants? A Study of Water Polluting Industries in India

detail.abstract: Whether the share of pollution control equipment stock in the total value of fixed assets is relatively higher in export-oriented Indian manufacturing plants than in similar plants not exporting is studied econometrically for water polluting industries in India. The analysis uses plant-level panel data from the Annual Survey of Industries for 2011 to 2019. The aim is to assess, indirectly, using data on assets, whether pollution abatement in Indian manufacturing plants in water-polluting industries is relatively greater among those participating in export markets than among non-exporting plants, as found in some earlier studies for other countries. The impact of ISO 14000 adoption on plants' investment in pollution-control equipment is also examined. The results of the analysis indicate that manufacturing plants in India that export have relatively larger stocks of pollution-control equipment than non-exporting plants. Additionally, a significant positive effect of ISO 14000 on investment in pollution-control equipment is observed.

תקציר בעברית: מאמר זה בוחן את כישלון האינטגרציה החרדית בישראל כמקרה בוחן של "פטור ללא השתתפות" - מסלול המנוגד לכישלון האינטגרציה המזרחי שנותח במאמר קודם (עובדיה, 2026). בעוד שהמזרחים סבלו מדרישה להתבוללות מוחלטת תוך הדרה מכוח מוסדי, החרדים קיבלו פטור כמעט מוחלט מליבת האזרחות הישראלית: שירות צבאי, חינוך ליבה, ותעסוקה. הסדר זה, שנועד במקור לאוכלוסייה קטנה של שרידי שואה, הפך לבסיס להתפתחות סדר נורמטיבי מקביל - מערכת שלמה של ערכים, סמכויות, ונאמנויות המתחרה עם זו של המדינה. המאמר טוען ששני המסלולים - "יותר מדי התערבות" (המקרה המזרחי) ו"פחות מדי התערבות" (המקרה החרדי) - מובילים לאותה תוצאה: משבר חוקתי המתפרץ דורות לאחר מכן. שני המשברים מתרחשים באותה חברה, באותו רגע (2023-2024), ומאיימים על יסודות הדמוקרטיה הישראלית. הלקח המרכזי הוא שאינטגרציה דורשת איזון - לא כפייה מוחלטת ולא פטור מוחלט, אלא משא ומתן מתמשך בין שמירה על זהות לבין השתתפות באזרחות משותפת.

English Abstract: This article examines the failure of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) integration in Israel as a case study of "exemption without participation"—a trajectory opposite to the Mizrahi integration failure analyzed in a companion article (Ovadia, 2026a). While Mizrahim suffered from a demand for complete assimilation while being excluded from institutional power, Haredim received near-total exemption from the core of Israeli citizenship: military service, core curriculum education, and employment. This arrangement, originally intended for a small population of Holocaust survivors, became the foundation for the development of a parallel normative order—a complete system of norms, values, and authorities competing with that of the state. The article argues that both trajectories—"too much intervention" (the Mizrahi case) and "too little intervention" (the Haredi case)—lead to the same outcome: constitutional crisis erupting generations later. Both crises are occurring in the same society, at the same moment (2023–2024), threatening the foundations of Israeli democracy. The 1948 Status Quo arrangement assumed the Haredi community would remain small and eventually disappear as secularism prevailed. This assumption proved catastrophically wrong: from approximately 60,000 in 1948 (400 military exemptions), the community grew to 1.2 million by 2024 (66,000+ exemptions), with exponential growth continuing due to high birth rates (7–8 children per family) and community closure. The exemption extended beyond military service to the entire core of citizenship: Haredi schools teach no secular subjects (mathematics, English, sciences, civics); male employment rates are the lowest in Israel (~50%); and half of Haredi families live below the poverty line, supported by government subsidies. Most critically, the Haredi community developed a parallel normative order: halakha (religious law) supersedes state law; rabbinic authority supersedes state authority; education cultivates communal rather than national loyalty. The 2024 Supreme Court ruling invalidating the military exemption triggered open refusal to comply with the court's decision—a constitutional crisis in the precise sense: when a segment of the population declares it will not obey the Supreme Court, and the government does not enforce the ruling, the rule of law itself is undermined. The central lesson: integration cannot be shortcut, neither through coercion nor through exemption. It requires balance—preservation of identity combined with participation in the core of citizenship. Not absolute assimilation and not absolute exemption, but ongoing negotiation between maintaining who you are and contributing to shared society. The alternative is to wait—and discover, 70 years later, that today's decisions created tomorrow's constitutional crisis.

English Abstract: This article synthesizes and integrates findings from two prior studies: "Unintentional Exclusion: The Mizrahi Case" (Ovadia, 2026a) and "The Exemption That Became a Parallel Order: The Haredi Case" (Ovadia, 2026b). Both studies documented integration failures in Israel that occurred during the same period (1948) but developed in opposite directions: Mizrahim suffered from "too much intervention" (a demand for assimilation while being excluded from power), while Haredim benefited from "too little intervention" (exemption from the core obligations of citizenship). The present article proposes a new analytical framework: the Opportunistic Asymmetry of Liberalism. The central argument is that both opposing failures stemmed from the same mechanism—a structural tendency of liberal systems to trample those who cooperate ("bullying the flexible") and capitulate to those who present determined resistance ("appeasing the rigid"). The Mizrahim, who arrived willing to integrate, were perceived as vulnerable and coercible; the Haredim, who presented refusal, received an exemption that continually expanded. Both opposite trajectories led to the same outcome: a constitutional crisis erupting 70–76 years after the founding decisions. The article traces the political legacy of this asymmetry, including an analysis of the "coalition funds" mechanism as an institutional continuation of the historical pattern. Finally, the article examines whether this pattern is unique to Israel or reflects a structural weakness of liberal democracies in general—a question of immediate relevance to contemporary Europe.

detail.abstract:
Background: The emergence of "Medical Child Welfare Task Forces" within pediatric tertiary centers has introduced a forensic surveillance model that increasingly pathologizes medical complexity. For families navigating rare, multisystemic conditions, the clinical environment is frequently transformed from a site of healing into a site of forensic scrutiny. 

Objective: This article deconstructs the systemic "decoupling" of Medical Child Abuse (MCA) from its psychiatric foundation, Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another (FDIA), and examines how this shift facilitates the criminalization of specialty-led medical management. 

Methods: Utilizing a dual perspective as a pediatric Registered Nurse and a parent with lived experience in a high-stakes forensic investigation, the author analyzes the "Forensic Retranscription" of clinical data. The analysis explores the role of the Electronic Medical Record (EMR) as a digital dragnet, the ethical implications of "information blocking" under 21st Century Cures Act exceptions, and the collapse of interoperability in complex care. * This manuscript is currently under peer review at the Journal of Pediatric Nursing. It is being shared via SSRN as a working paper to facilitate scholarly dialogue and provide immediate access to the clinical and ethical frameworks discussed herein. Please cite as a "Working Paper" or "Preprint." Criminalization of Complexity 2.

Results: The study identifies a recurring pattern where objective specialty diagnoses (e.g.,MCAS, EDS, Mitochondrial disease) are systematically erased by forensic evaluators through "sensitive" EMR notations and the suppression of specialist-verified records. This diagnostic "shadow-system" circumvents the legal requirement of proven deception, instead reframing diagnostic disputes and second opinions as indicators of abuse. 

Conclusions: The current forensic framework creates a moral hazard by leveraging "GoodFaith Immunity" to override evidence-based medicine. To restore diagnostic integrity and patient safety, the author proposes mandatory rare disease specialist consultations in MCA evaluations and a return to radical transparency in the EMR. Nurses are uniquely positioned to advocate for these safeguards, mitigating the institutional trauma caused by the forensic pathologization of organic disease.

detail.abstract: This article explores the trend in digital financial inclusion during war. It also explores the importance and challenges of digital financial inclusion during war. War and armed conflict adversely affect people. Their struggle to survive the war becomes even more difficult when they are unable to visit a bank branch to access formal financial services during war due to lockdowns and curfews that lead to the closure of physical financial access points. This study gathers insights from war data and show that the use of digital financial services increased during war. The study also suggests some strategies for increasing the level of digital financial inclusion during war. The insights offered in this study can assist policymakers and financial service providers in ensuring that people in conflict zones have access to digital financial services to meet their subsistence and survival needs during war.

detail.title: Can Universities Advance Equity Under Constraint?

publicationDetails.detailsText: 2026 Forthcoming, Archiv des Völkerrechts (Archives of International Law)

detail.abstract: SDG 4 calls for inclusive and equitable quality education, yet universities across the Global North face contracting resources rather than expanding ones. The intuitive response is retrenchment. Some institutions, however, have advanced equity not despite constraint but through deliberate redesign. This article asks whether equity can advance under constraint, and if so, how. It identifies certain design requirements that distinguish institutions that narrow equity gaps from those that widen them. The article then examines how policy can support equity-advancing design, while recognising that policy cannot substitute for institutional commitment. When resources contract, whether equity advances or retreats depends on how institutions are designed.

title: Forecasting Oil Volatility through Network Models with GARCH-Informed Correlation Weights
affiliations: University of Bejaia, University of Bejaia, Cardiff University and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Forecasting Oil Volatility through Network Models with GARCH-Informed Correlation Weights
detail.abstract: This study addresses the computational challenges of forecasting volatility in highdimensional commodity markets. Building on the Network log-ARCH framework, we introduce a novel class of network topologies from GARCH-informed correlation weights, obtained from conditional covariance estimates of multivariate GARCH models, rather than relying on the heuristic distance measures commonly used in clustering methods. We evaluate the proposed models forecasting performance through a rolling-window exercise using a panel of OPEC members crude oil prices. The results identify network volatility models incorporating these new GARCHinformed weights as the statistically superior specifications. Remarkably, the proposed framework matches standard DCC-GARCH predictive accuracy while delivering up to 62,000-fold computational gains. By explicitly modeling contemporaneous spillovers through interpretable spatial ARCH-like lags estimated via GMM, the proposed approach offers an optimal trade-off between parsimony, interpretability, and performance. The findings establish GARCH-informed network models as robust, scalable alternatives for systemic risk measurement and volatility forecasting in interconnected financial markets.

detail.title: Beyond Banks: Trust Among the Financially Underserved

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-06
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In 2023, over 18 percent of US households were either unbanked or underbanked, a group commonly referred to as financially underserved (e.g., see Burhouse, Navarro and Osaki (2016)). Prior work and survey evidence identify a lack of broad-scope trust in banks as an important reason for financial exclusion (e.g., FDIC (2024), Falcettoni and Nygaard (2025), and Xu (2020)). Yet it is not clear whether this mistrust is unique to banks or whether it extends to other institutions, such as government entities or nonbank providers of account services. This distinction matters for policymakers when considering how to serve this segment of the population. If mistrust is specific to banks, then alternative providers of account services — such as nonbanks or government entities — could improve access to the financial system. But if mistrust extends to alternative providers, then financial education or other trust-building initiatives might be more effective at increasing financial inclusion.

To address this gap, we designed our own surveys and fielded them to a sample of unbanked and underbanked individuals in the US. We elicited their levels of trust in various institutions, including different types of banks, government-related entities, and alternative payment providers. Using principal component analysis, we identify three dominant components of the trust scores which we label, in descending order of importance: (1) broad-scope trust, (2) concerns about traditional financial institutions, and (3) preference for a physical business presence. We explore how sociodemographic characteristics, including income, age, education, race and political affiliation, affect these components of trust.

title: The Hidden Cost of Flexibility: Decomposing the WFH Productivity Premium into Efficiency versus Unpaid Hours

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Flexibility: Decomposing the WFH Productivity Premium into Efficiency versus Unpaid Hours
detail.abstract: Remote workers appear more productive, but only when productivity is measured per day. I show that this apparent premium masks a more complex reality. Using minute-by-minute time diary data from the American Time Use Survey (2019-2024, N = 19,228), I decompose the work-from-home (WFH) productivity premium into a true efficiency component (earnings per hour worked) and a hours channel (longer working days). The central finding reverses a common narrative: WFH workers are far more efficient per hour than the headline daily premium suggests, not less. The WFH efficiency premium is 0.42 log points per hour, more than five times the 0.08 log-point headline premium per day. This gap arises because WFH workers log 2.9 additional hours per diary day, of which 2.6 hours constitute "invisible overtime" exceeding self-reported usual schedules. These additional hours dilute rather than inflate the daily premium. The pattern is robust across ten specifications, an instrumental variables strategy exploiting occupation-level teleworkability, and a difference-indifferences design. Heterogeneity analysis reveals an equity dimension: women log the most additional hours (2.9 per diary day) yet capture the lowest headline premium (0.13 log points for mothers), while men without children achieve the highest headline returns (0.18 log points) with fewer additional hours. These findings reframe the policy debate: WFH does not merely redistribute existing work across locations; it fundamentally expands the working day, with uneven consequences across the demographic spectrum.

title: Linking Operational Initiatives to Realized Financial Outcomes in Private Equity Transformations

detail.title: Linking Operational Initiatives to Realized Financial Outcomes in Private Equity Transformations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The views expressed are those of the author alone and do not represent the positions of any current or former employer, client, or affiliated organization.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Private equity-backed transformations operate under conditions that differ fundamentally from those faced by large corporates pursuing internally funded change programs. Ownership horizons are compressed, accountability for financial performance is immediate, and value creation must ultimately be validated through external diligence at exit.

Despite these constraints, many transformation efforts rely on parallel measurement systems that track initiative activity and modeled benefits outside the company’s statutory financial reporting framework. This disconnect often produces ambiguity regarding whether the operational improvements have been translated into durable economic outcomes. Such separation undermines management confidence, weakens governance, and exposes valuation risk during the sale processes.

This article proposes a practical framework for linking transformation initiatives directly to realized enterprise value reflected in the profit and loss statement, balance sheet, and cash flow of the enterprise. Rather than treating transformation tracking as a separate analytical discipline, the framework embeds initiative measurement within financial reality through explicit baselines, conservative attribution rules, and governance mechanisms designed to reconcile planned and realized outcomes. The framework complements standard private equity value-creation playbooks by providing a disciplined method for validating that initiatives translate into realized enterprise value.

The approach emphasizes speed of deployment, repeatability across heterogeneous portfolio companies, and evidentiary credibility under diligence conditions, while acknowledging the data limitations typical of newly acquired assets. The proposed framework is intended to reduce valuation leakage at exit by ensuring that operational improvements are demonstrable in audited financial statements rather than supported only by management projections.

The article argues that reliable transformation tracking constitutes a core operating capability for private equity sponsors rather than a project-specific tool. When architecture, measurement mechanics, data discipline, and governance cadence are aligned with statutory performance, transformation shifts from a narrative of projected savings to a demonstrable alteration of the company’s economic trajectory. Firms that institutionalize such frameworks can accelerate value realization during ownership, improve decision-making under uncertainty, and present more defensible earnings bridges at exit, thereby converting operational improvement into durable equity value.

In dedicated chapters or elsewhere, Korea's FTAs typically contain provisions on environmental protection ranging from general exceptions to more specific provisions that prevent relaxation of environmental laws, recognize the right to regulate, encourage public participation in tackling environmental matters, set forth sustainable development commitments, promote environmental cooperation, establish specialized institutional mechanisms and so on. The breadth and depth of environmental provisions vary from agreement to agreement. This chapter aims to review and identify main characteristics and patterns of environmental regulation across Korea's FTAs and draw out key messages for addressing trade-environment issues.

detail.abstract: The issue of fisheries subsidies has garnered significant attention within the global community due to its multifaceted implications for both economic development and environmental sustainability. Adopted at the 12th Ministerial Conference of the Word Trade Organization (WTO) in 2022, a new Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (AFS) aims to prevent governments from using certain subsidies that lead to unsustainable fishing practices. As the first WTO environmental agreement, the AFS differs from the existing WTO disciplines on industrial subsidies by focusing on environmental protection and preservation rather than countering trade distortions. This chapter discusses the negotiation history and main provisions of the AFS as well as its relevance to the Central Asian and other landlocked country members. It concludes that, despite the limited direct impact of the AFS on these countries, their full participation will support global sustainability efforts and help meet their domestic demand for fish products.

title: Trust in Regulation in a Time of Revolution
affiliations: Peter A. Allard School of Law

detail.title: Trust in Regulation in a Time of Revolution
detail.abstract:
In a moment when big-P Politics feel practically catastrophic, the suggestion that we should be focusing on regulation could seem foolish, or worse: it could seem like some kind of self-serving effort to pretend our work rearranging deck chairs continues to matter. Regulation can feel like the opposite of resistance, and resistance is on many peoples’ minds these days, particularly in the United States. And, the goal of this paper is to argue that failing to focus on regulation – and especially on trust in regulation, in this time of revolution – would be a terrible mistake. Regulation is at the leading edge of politics in a way we sometimes fail to recognize. Regulation is where the “rubber” of policy and aspiration meets the “road” of implementation and subject-facing engagement. Regulation is the face of government for most people in their daily lives.

This article examines trust in regulation as a core value and precondition of the modern liberal democratic regulatory state. It develops a concept of justified trust in regulation, grounded in regulatory trustworthiness—honesty, competence, and reliability—rather than in proxies such as partisan loyalty, blind faith, obedience, or resignation. The article situates this conception of regulatory trustworthiness within liberal democratic rule‑of‑law commitments to equal respect, fairness, and accountability, and shows how it underpinned late‑twentieth‑century imaginings of the “regulatory state.” It then contrasts this model with an emerging illiberal vision, exemplified by the current American President’s emphasis on personal loyalty, in‑group allegiance, and zero‑sum politics – all of which actively repudiate the conditions for justified trust. Using regulatory theory and examples from contemporary US governance, the article argues that mutual justified trust between regulators and regulated actors is an indispensable “capital good” for effective, flexible, and fair regulatory regimes. It concludes that rebuilding a functional regulatory state after an illiberal turn requires explicitly naming, protecting, and measuring regulatory trustworthiness as a central liberal value, alongside the rule of law, democratic accountability, and a basic commitment to equality.

title: Severe Weather and Financial (In)stability

detail.title: Severe Weather and Financial (In)stability

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We quantify the effect of severe weather shocks on the US economy in an environment in which the economy can switch between periods of financial stability and financial instability, like the Great Recession. We estimate a New Keynesian dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with banks and severe weather events. We show that severe weather shocks: 1) have a negative impact on real and financial US variables, sizable only in periods of financial instability, but muted effects on nominal variables; 2) are never a relevant source of business cycles fluctuations; 3) transmit mainly via a deterioration in the quality of capital.

detail.title: Anticorruption Framework and Nigeria's Sustainability
detail.abstract: Corruption involves activities without transparency and accountability aiming at personal benefit at the expense of others. It undermines the intentions of government and also creates opportunities for the miscarriage of justice. This bad condition can be curbed through anticorruption war driven by political will to promote national integrity and sustainability. Political will does not exist in a vacuum but can be located primarily in the legislature and other relevant institutions established to fight it. Essentially, anticorruption incorporates measures to institute checks and balances within the government and relevant institutions against corruption or perceived corrupt practices. Thus, anticorruption measures and sustainability can thrive on demonstrating political will in sufficient frequency in a highly corrupt environment over flowing with poverty. The case for institutionalizing effective anticorruption measures in a country like Nigeria where serving public officers can steal trillions of naira through many fronts, cannot be overemphasized. The investigation literature review research design was adopted for the study and the result showed significant positive relationship between anticorruption measures and sustainability. The study was not exhaustive due to lack of relevant current literature in these areas and research funding. Further study can examine the relationship between corruption and homelessness among low income public servants in Nigeria. The study recommends that the Senate Committee on Anticorruption and Financial Crimes should ensure the passing into law of Senator Adebule's Proceeds of Crime (Recovery and Management Bill 2025) to improve transparency and accountability in the handling of recovered public funds from criminals in power.

title: Populistic Surfing: Consensus, Monetary and Banking Policies
affiliations: Bocconi University - BAFFI Center on International Markets, Money, and Regulation and Bocconi University - Department of Economics, Bocconi University - Department of Economics (ECO)

detail.title: Populistic Surfing: Consensus, Monetary and Banking Policies

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This chapter, using a political economy approach, uncovers the relationships between populism, on the one side, and monetary and banking policies, on the other side. The analysis is based on three assumptions. First, both monetary and banking policies can produce redistributive effects. Second, political consensus can be associated with redistribution. Third, populists, being politicians, are myopic players, hence heavily influenced by citizens' financial and group heterogeneities. Given these assumptions, two different models are studied. Concerning monetary policies, a nexus between populism and central bank (in)dependence (CBI) can emerge where the populist aim to influence the monetary policy design after a macroeconomic shock that requires public bailouts. Regarding banking policy, our chapter defines populism as Democratic Rioting, in which citizens are assumed to be heavily influenced in their policy choice by psychological group dynamics. This explains why populist consensus emerges and may deliver different policy choices depending on non-banking news such as public welfare choices and immigration.

title: Improving Organ Procurement Operations
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Improving Organ Procurement Operations

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study how decisions made by organ procurement organizations (OPOs)—non-profits that coordinate organ recovery from deceased donors—affect the availability of organs for transplant in the United States. We develop a structural econometric model of a pivotal OPO decision: whether to approach a potential donor’s family to request authorization for donation. Our model conceptualizes this decision in two parts. The OPO first estimates the probabilities of two downstream outcomes: authorization (i.e., family consent) and transplant (i.e., whether the donated organs would be successfully transplanted). It then applies a cost-benefit decision rule that maps these estimates to an approach decision. Our model separately identifies the OPO’s beliefs (i.e., probability estimates), its preferences (i.e., costs / benefits), and the true probabilities of authorization and transplant. We apply our model to a dataset of 35,856 potential donors referred to four OPOs between 2016 and 2021. We find that OPOs missed a substantial number of donation opportunities, recovering organs from only 39% of transplantable donors. Of these missed opportunities, an estimated 16% resulted from conservative preferences, 12% from miscalibrated beliefs, and the remaining 72% from family declines. We conduct a detailed counterfactual policy evaluation to identify impactful and actionable changes to OPO decisions. We find that drastically increasing approach rates would allow OPOs to recover organs from 43% more donors, creating over $100 million in additional annual societal benefit.
