detail.title: At the Crossroads of Compliance and Care: The Question of Power in Trauma-Informed Care Implementation in Child and Youth Residential Care
detail.abstract: Trauma-informed care (TIC) emerged in response to recognition that service systems can reproduce harm through coercion and unexamined power imbalances. Yet empirical research suggests that TIC implementation often fails to meaningfully interrogate power, particularly within child- and youth-serving sectors (CYSSs), where compliance-oriented practices are widely normalized. This study examines how adult–child power dynamics shape TIC implementation in child and youth residential care, a setting where therapeutic intervention, discipline, and daily life intersect under conditions of heightened institutional control. Using a constructivist grounded theory approach, an in-depth qualitative study was conducted within a large urban residential care agency implementing TIC in Québec, Canada. Data included 17 in-depth interviews with staff across roles and organizational levels, 45 hours of participant observation of trainings, clinical support activities, and leadership meetings, and analysis of implementation and institutional documents. Analysis generated four theoretical categories tracing how trauma-informed and compliance-oriented logics coexist and interact: (1) a legacy of harsh and rigid compliance-oriented approaches, (2) earlier relational shifts that created openings for TIC, (3) the continued presence of compliance-oriented practices, and (4) a continuum of TIC uptake ranging from relational alignment to carceral resistance. TIC supported more relational shifts where prior cultural change had already unsettled compliance-based assumptions. Where behaviourist or carceral mandates remained entrenched, TIC was taken up selectively or framed as an add-on, preserving dominant logics of authority, risk management, and behavioural control. Findings suggest that TIC implementation in CYSSs cannot be understood apart from the broader normalization of adult dominance over children. Without explicitly addressing childism and the organizational conditions required to shift power, TIC risks being absorbed into compliance-oriented frameworks rather than producing transformative change.

detail.abstract: Background: Pricing is a core mechanic for the adoption of AI-based clinical decision support systems (CDSS). Using an AI-enabled CDSS for cardiovascular risk, we examined how pricing structures shape stakeholder acceptance and perceived adoption barriers.Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional, anonymous survey with N=371 clinicians, managers, IT specialists, researchers, and policy stakeholders with exposure to CDSS applications. The instrument elicited preferences regarding primary cost-bearers, product packaging, acceptability of specific pricing models (one-time, subscription, usage-based, outcome-based; algorithm-only vs. bundled), perceived adoption barriers, and willingness to pilot. Descriptive statistics were used for categorical outcomes, and mean ranks were calculated for barrier prioritization. Qualitative free-text responses were coded thematically.Results: Hospitals and clinics were the preferred primary cost-bearer (45.0%). As a product packaging option, the full bundle consists of an AI-derived risk score, a clinical decision support system (CDSS), and a patient-facing citizen app. This option was most frequently rated as providing the greatest value (34.8%), although uncertainty remained high (43.7%). Among pricing options, a one-time license for the full bundle showed the highest acceptability (31.7% very acceptable); outcome-based pricing ranked second (27.6% very acceptable) but elicited more polarized responses. Participants mentioned unclear return on investment (ROI; mean rank 2.65), followed by concerns about subscription-based pricing (3.03) and integration complexity (3.14) as the most important acceptance barriers. Interestingly, “overall pricing too high” ranked lowest in importance (6.38). Overall, 64.4% of respondents reported openness to piloting, conditional on costs and value demonstration.Conclusions: These findings indicate that pricing structure, rather than absolute price level, primarily influences adoption by shaping budget predictability, risk sharing, and perceived ROI. We derive practical guidance prioritizing demonstrable ROI and predictable, yet flexible pricing options.

detail.title: Job preferences for modifiable hospital working conditions among Dutch nurses: a discrete choice experiment

keywords.keywords: Discrete choice experimentEmployment conditionsWorking conditionsNursing professionRetentionIntention to leaveTurnover

detail.abstract: Background: While the demand for nurses is increasing, a considerable proportion of nurses considers leaving their current job. Little is known about nurses’ views on changeable aspects of hospital working conditions.Objective: To investigate nurses’ preferences for modifiable hospital working conditions, and estimate nurses’ relative utility trade-offs between certain working conditions and salary changes.Design: A discrete choice experiment (DCE) surveySetting(s): The NetherlandsParticipants: 966 Dutch nurses who either obtained or are obtaining a nursing degree and used to or are currently working as a nurse.Methods: Each participant was repeatedly asked to choose between three alternatives; two hospital nursing jobs with eight different modifiable working conditions (attributes) and an opt-out. The eight attributes were: salary, scheduling, professional development, influence in the organisation, support with work strain, social engagement, nature of work and organisation of work. The data were analysed using a mixed logit model, based on outcomes predicted uptake and relative utility trade-off calculations.Results: The mixed logit model and choice share predictions showed that higher wages (€2700 and €3500 versus €2200), more predictable scheduling (monthly and quarterly versus weekly scheduling), and influence within the organisation (departmental and organisational versus no influence)  substantially increased the likelihood of accepting a nursing hospital job.  Improvements in the attributes time for professional development, support with work strain, social engagement, and organisation of work led to a modest increase in this likelihood, whereas deteriorations led to pronounced declines. Preference-heterogeneity for these attributes was high, which implies that different nurses have different preferences for these working conditions. The opt‑out dispersion interval was notably wide, further indicating nurses’ sensitivity to unattractive job profiles.Conclusions: Hospitals aiming to reduce turnover rates among nurses should prioritise salary and scheduling reforms while simultaneously offering flexible employment packages that accommodate diverse preferences regarding influence, support, and organisation of work. Avoiding unattractive working conditions may be as effective as increasing salary alone.

title: Food, Brain, and Performance: The Science Behind Food for Mood

detail.title: Food, Brain, and Performance: The Science Behind Food for Mood

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The concepts presented are part of the author’s broader educational work in workplace health and public health communication.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and literature based analysis and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. Institutional ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a science-based framework for understanding energy, focus, and mood in the modern workforce through a biological lens. While workplace performance is often framed as a behavioral or motivational challenge, a growing body of peer-reviewed research suggests that physiological factors play a foundational role in cognitive endurance and emotional stability. Nutrient availability, glycemic dynamics, neurotransmitter activity, and gut–brain signaling systems all influence how individuals experience mental clarity, fatigue, and resilience across the workday.

Drawing from research in nutrition science, neuroscience, and metabolic health, this paper explores how dietary patterns function as biological signals that shape cognitive tempo and mood regulation. Evidence indicates that macronutrient composition, micronutrient sufficiency, and plant-derived compounds can measurably influence alertness, stress response, and perceived wellbeing. Large-scale intake data further suggest that many adults fall short in key nutrients associated with cognitive and metabolic function, highlighting a potential gap in current workplace wellness strategies.

The paper introduces a “biology-first” model for workforce wellbeing that emphasizes plain language education, functional self awareness, and privacy respecting insights. Rather than positioning performance as a matter of willpower alone, this framework reframes energy and focus as partially biological phenomena that can be supported through accessible, real world interventions.

By integrating biological literacy into wellness conversations, organizations may be able to improve sustained energy, cognitive clarity, and engagement while reducing stigma around fatigue and burnout. This framework offers a practical, scalable complement to traditional behavior focused wellness models.

title: Air or Sea? Quality-Driven Sorting in International Trade
affiliations: University of Turin and Universita di Cagliari

detail.title: Air or Sea? Quality-Driven Sorting in International Trade
detail.abstract: We study how product quality shapes the choice between air and sea freight. In a model with non-homothetic demand and income uncertainty, exporters face a timing wedge: sea shipments must commit quantities before uncertainty resolves, whereas air shipments can be better timed but at a higher cost. The model predicts sharp modal sorting for vertically differentiated goods—high-quality varieties fly, lower-quality varieties sail—and that the average air–sea quality (unit-value) gap shrinks as sea routes lengthen relative to air routes. Using U.S. customs data at the exporter–district–product level, we confirm both patterns. Exploiting within-route time variation in relative freight costs in a 2SLS design, we show that higher sea costs (relative to air) increase the average unit value of air shipments, consistent with re-sorting by quality. Calibrated counterfactuals quantify how volatility, COVID-type air-cost disruptions, and tariff-type marginal-cost shocks reshape participation, mode choice, and profits across routes.

title: Open-Source Media and Marketing Mix Modeling: Practice-Oriented Overview, Challenges, Opportunities
affiliations: Northwestern University and

detail.title: Open-Source Media and Marketing Mix Modeling: Practice-Oriented Overview, Challenges, Opportunities
detail.abstract: Privacy-enhancing technologies are reshaping online advertising, making it increasingly difficult for advertisers to track customer journeys and link marketing actions to economic outcomes. As a result, interest in probabilistic measurement techniques such as media and marketing mix modeling (m/MMM) has surged, particularly among digital-first advertisers. Many of these advertisers are small and midsize firms that rely heavily on digital channels yet lack the resources to commission bespoke proprietary models. Against this backdrop, grassroots analytics communities and large online advertising platforms such as Meta Platforms and Google have started developing opensource packages for m/MMM. The packages share core principles but differ on important aspects such as their degree of automation, ease of use, and modeling paradigms. This article provides a narrative review and practice-oriented synthesis of these developments and discusses the challenges and opportunities that come with "packaged up" m/MMM. It concludes with an outline of topics that marketing scholars can engage with to vet and extend open-source m/MMM, and to align its continued development with its users' needs.

detail.title: Corporate Value(S)

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Penn, Inst for Law & Econ Research Paper No. 26-04
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Values have always been a part of corporate operations, but they are particularly salient today. Corporate values now weigh heavily in consumer, employee, and shareholder choices, so much so that misaligned values can make or break companies. Some argue that managers should select values that align with those of their stakeholders. Others argue that corporate values should match shareholder preferences. Still others claim that economic value, without regard to values, should be the sole focus of managerial efforts. The debate over values is not only important for the theory and practice of corporate governance, but also carries significant policy implications, as Congress and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are poised to deconstruct the shareholder proposal mechanism—a key source of corporate values formation—based on a limited appreciation of the role of values in corporate operations. 

In this Article, we set out to align those who highlight the importance of values with those who maintain that a corporation’s proper role is to focus on value. We argue that managers should select the corporate values that maximize long-term economic value. To do so, however, managers need to understand the economic significance of corporate values. Understanding the values of corporate stakeholders is a key input in that assessment. It is relatively easy for most stakeholders—consumers, employees and even the government—to communicate their values to corporations. Consumers, for instance, do so through their purchasing decisions and, in more extreme cases, boycotts. Employees choose jobs based on values and communicate their preferences to management through internal channels. Shareholders, however, lack ready ways to communicate their values, disadvantaging them relative to other stakeholders, and leaving managers with an information gap that can lead to costly mistakes. 

We leverage the foregoing analysis to advocate against two potentially transformative trends in shareholder democracy—the pressure on the shareholder proposal rule and the adoption of voting choice programs. First, the power of public company shareholders to introduce shareholder proposals, many of which deal with values-related issues, has inspired a powerful backlash. Congress is considering repeal of the shareholder proposal rule, and the Chairman of the SEC has expressed frustrated with environmental, social and governance (ESG)-related proposals and backed a controversial proposition that precatory proposals are illegal under state law. Our analysis shows that repealing the shareholder proposal rule or banning values-based proposals would be a mistake in that precatory proposals provide a focused and transparent mechanism for management to learn about what their shareholders value (and what they consider unimportant) without interfering with board discretion. Instead of a ban, we recommend tailored modifications to the rule to address the concerns about misuse that have given rise to its condemnation. 

Second, in response to political pressure and criticisms of their stewardship activities, the Big Three mutual funds (Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street) have implemented voting choice programs, whereby they delegate voting decisions for their portfolio companies to their mutual fund customers by allowing them to select from a curated menu of voting policies. We argue that this approach is flawed. Rather, financial intermediaries should retain their voting power but inform their voting decisions by actively soliciting input from their customers about their values and views. Intermediary stewardship is a more effective way to convey shareholder values to management as long as it is informed by the views of funds’ economic owners.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in High-Growth Companies of the Agro-Industrial Complex
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in High-Growth Companies of the Agro-Industrial Complex
detail.abstract: High-growth companies play a key role in the structural transformation of the economy, becoming centers of job generation and innovation. Maintaining rapid growth in the agro-industrial complex is particularly important for ensuring national food security. The article examines the application of artificial intelligence technologies in highgrowth companies of the agro-industrial complex as a tool for enhancing efficiency and competitiveness. Based on an analysis of academic publications, industry research, and corporate information, three main areas of artificial intelligence implementation are identified: predictive analytics based on satellite imagery and machine learning algorithms for field monitoring and yield forecasting; automation of production processes through the development of autonomous control systems for agricultural machinery; and intelligent livestock monitoring using computer vision. The article presents specific examples of artificial intelligence technology implementation in companies of the agro-industrial complex (Taranis, Ceres AI, CropX, Ever.ag, John Deere). It is concluded that the implementation of artificial intelligence technologies enables high-growth companies to increase competitiveness, optimize management decisions, and reduce the labor intensity of production processes.

title: Europeanisation of the Polish Law on Administrative Enforcement Proceedings

detail.title: Europeanisation of the Polish Law on Administrative Enforcement Proceedings
detail.abstract: The article presents a description of the convergence of the Polish law on administrative enforcement proceedings with the corresponding EU legal framework. The presented analysis shows how Polish administrative law is mainly shaped by the harmonisation process that is occurring on the EU level. The legal mechanisms introduced by various European directives have been implemented into two Polish laws: the Administrative Enforcement Proceedings Act and the Mutual Assistance Act. Both laws have introduced new solutions and mechanisms which changed the old Polish framework and lead to the introduction of new, and previously unknown, legal institutions into Polish administrative enforcement proceedings law.

detail.abstract: Framework agreements are widely used in public procurement to provide flexibility while maintaining competitive pricing. This chapter explores how framework agreements can be designed as a menu of contracts, allowing contracting authorities to choose between different price-quality combinations. We analyze the trade-offs inherent in this approach — in particular how offering flexibility of choice to the contracting authority affects the competitive dynamics of procurement. The analysis draws on screening theory to show how a well-designed menu can improve allocative efficiency by matching heterogeneous needs to appropriate contractual terms.

detail.title: Bottom of the Pyramid Theory of Financial Inclusion: Understanding How Financial Inclusion Reduces Economic Inequality

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Economic Exploitation and Inequality, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: The aim of this article is to develop a theory that explains how the actions of people at the bottom of the pyramid (BOP) enable financial inclusion in the BOP segment of the economic pyramid. It highlights the conditions that enable financial inclusion to take place in the BOP segment. The bottom of the pyramid theory of financial inclusion states that the provision of appropriate financial services to people at the bottom of the pyramid can help to meet their needs, improve their wellbeing and reduce their incentive to engage in antisocial actions that destabilize industries, markets and society. The theory offers seven predictions or hypotheses. One, there are unbanked adults with unmet basic needs. Two, they will use interaction with social networks to demand appropriate financial services. Three, they have incentives to use antisocial methods to ensure that their demands are met if ignored. Four, to avoid this, the authorities and financial service providers will work collaboratively to ensure adequate provision of appropriate financial services for them. Five, such intervention will discourage unbanked adults from undertaking antisocial actions. Six, unbanked adults will use financial services as a bridge to transition from the bottom of the pyramid to a higher level of the economic pyramid, thereby reducing economic inequality. Seven, the use of financial services and the quality of financial decision making will determine whether banked adults will transition to a higher level of the economic pyramid or remain at the bottom of the pyramid.

detail.title: Mapping the Nanotechnology Landscape in Healthcare: A Multi-Domain Analysis of Scientific Output, Innovation, Clinical Trials, and Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: Nanotechnology is transforming healthcare by enabling precise molecular-scale manipulation to develop innovative diagnostic and therapeutic solutions. This study integrates bibliometric mapping (2014–2024), patent landscape analysis, clinical trial evaluation, and market forecasting to present a comprehensive view of nano-healthcare. Bibliometric data show a threefold rise in publications (4,321 to 15,081) and a surge in average citations per paper (1.19 to 54.97). Clinical trials of nanoparticle-based therapies expanded fifty-five-fold since 2000, with Phase II studies dominating and oncology comprising over 90% of investigations. Patent filings and grants nearly quadrupled, while median grant-lag times halved post-2018, indicating faster translation. Harmonized market forecasts project growth from USD 232.5 billion in 2024 to USD 493.9 billion by 2030 (CAGR 12.4%), supported by 1,318 catalogued products. A SWOT analysis highlights opportunities in non-oncology applications, regulatory harmonization, and emerging markets, alongside challenges in safety, scalability, and regional disparities, offering a strategic framework for stakeholders to accelerate innovation.

detail.abstract: Since 1958, the European Commission has been in charge of controlling State aids. The interpretation by the CJEU of Articles 107 to 109 TFEU has been such that almost all advantages granted to certain undertakings by public entities are covered by the concept of State aid. That means that, in principle, they must all be notified to and authorized by the European Commission. Taking into account the amount of aids granted each year in the EU and the number of notifications potentially received by the European Commission, considering that every year new kinds of unlawful aids are exposed and bearing in mind the perception by legal scholars that many unlawful aids are not, and will likely never be, discovered by the Commission, one can wonder whether it makes sense to involve domestic competition authorities in State aids control. This chapter will test this hypothesis with reference to the Portuguese Competition Authority.

detail.abstract: This study examines public procurement in Russia's construction sector, highlighting its deep entrenchment in corruption and state patronage. Based on 50 interviews with 27 business and state officials, we find that authorities enable corruption and tax evasion for self-enrichment and power consolidation. Contrary to claims that digitalisation curbs corruption in public procurement, we argue that state patronage sustains a cycle of illegal practices. A weak judiciary reinforces corruption, increasing state intervention, eroding public trust, and lowering tax compliance. As a result, corruption remains socially accepted, making meaningful reform unlikely.

title: Ethics and Corporate Governance in Modern Accounting
affiliations: University of Ghana - University of Ghana Business School (UGBS)

detail.title: Ethics and Corporate Governance in Modern Accounting
detail.abstract: This research examines the relationship between ethics and governance in the accounting discipline, specifically how certain ethical principles are incorporated into governance and its associated practices. Utilizing the structured literature review method, this paper reviews previous studies in academia and the professional sector that focus on the intersections of ethics, corporate governance, and accounting supervision. The work examines both seminal and contemporary literature to identify patterns, theories, and empirical contributions regarding the place of ethics in governance. The examination reveals that the governance of systems can be enhanced through the incorporation of specific ethics, including the enhancement of reporting quality, the reduction of opportunistic behavior, and the improvement of stakeholder confidence. Prior studies show that ethical breaches are central to failures in governance, yet strong ethical standards correlate with positive governance in monitoring, decision making, and control (Rezaee, 2008; Agrawal and Chadha, 2005). It is also evident that ethics is not only a compliance issue but also a regulative framework that influences the governance and its sustainability positively (Bebbington and Unerman, 2018). This implies that ethics in accounting governance is not only auxiliary or reactionary, and this should inform policies, practices, and research agendas. This is the response to the research question for this study.

title: Adoption of Energy-Efficient Technologies in Manufacturing to Minimize Carbon Emissions and Operational Costs
affiliations: University of Bergen

detail.title: Adoption of Energy-Efficient Technologies in Manufacturing to Minimize Carbon Emissions and Operational Costs
detail.abstract: This research paper investigates the implementation and effectiveness of energy-efficient technologies in the manufacturing sector, focusing on their potential to minimize carbon emissions and reduce operational costs. As global concerns regarding climate change intensify, the manufacturing industry faces increasing pressure to adopt sustainable practices. This study analyzes various energy-efficient technologies, including advanced automation systems, renewable energy integrations, and energy management systems, assessing their impact on operational efficiency and environmental performance. Through case studies and quantitative analysis, we demonstrate how these technologies not only lower greenhouse gas emissions but also contribute to significant cost savings over time. Furthermore, we explore the barriers to adoption and identify best practices for successful integration. The findings highlight the dual benefits of energy-efficient technologies: enhancing competitiveness while supporting sustainability goals, thereby providing insights for policymakers, industry leaders, and academic researchers aiming to advance sustainable manufacturing practices.

The work outlines the aerodynamic configuration, structural materials, propulsion concepts, and integrated avionics that define the MAR17 platform, emphasizing stealth geometry, energy efficiency, and mission adaptability. The book explores how advanced autonomy, AI-assisted decision systems, and modular payload integration can enhance precision, situational awareness, and operational flexibility in modern aerial missions. Special attention is given to multidomain interoperability, allowing the platform to coordinate with broader defense and security ecosystems. Beyond technical aspects, the MAR17 is framed as part of a forward-looking vision for UAV evolution, where intelligent systems, adaptive design, and human-machine collaboration redefine aerial strategy. This publication serves as both a conceptual blueprint and a strategic pers.

title: When the Classroom Becomes the Conflict Zone: Clinical ADR Education as a Multilevel Transformation Agent

detail.title: When the Classroom Becomes the Conflict Zone: Clinical ADR Education as a Multilevel Transformation Agent

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Legal Education, Volume 74, No. 2/3

detail.abstract:
Twenty years after Carrie Menkel-Meadow's transformative 2004 Journal of Legal Education article reshaped dispute resolution pedagogy, this case study demonstrates how her vision operates during institutional crisis. This article examines how clinical legal education in Alternative/Appropriate Dispute Resolution (ADR) served as both a theoretical foundation and practical instrument for addressing acute intercommunal tensions at the University of Haifa Faculty of Law following the October 7, 2023, attacks. Menkel-Meadow’s seminal piece, “From Legal Disputes to Conflict Resolution and Human Problem Solving: Legal Dispute Resolution in a Multidisciplinary Context,” advocating for human-centered legal education, process pluralism, and practice-based ADR education, created a bold vision that this case study shows could prove to be crucial for addressing conflict within academic institutions themselves.

At Haifa Law Faculty, where Menkel-Meadow's visits directly influenced the establishment of our Dispute Resolution Clinic, her vision was put to the test when the classroom became the conflict zone. Our case represents a three-level implementation of her principles: individual (students and faculty applying ADR to their own concerns regarding safety and academic freedom), professional (clinic students and ADR clinician transitioning from mediating and spreading ADR tools for members of disadvantaged populations, to implementing their theoretical and practical knowledge inside their community), and societal (creating a replicable model for managing ethno-national tensions in academic institutions).

The analysis illustrates how Menkel-Meadow's framework creates a self-reinforcing cycle: the clinical infrastructure established based on her theories later became essential for resolving conflicts within the institution. It also demonstrates the limits of consent-based approaches when addressing entrenched ideological divisions, while acknowledging their capacity to create dialogue opportunities and prevent escalation. We offer insights into the transformative potential of clinical ADR education across individual, professional, and societal levels, ultimately validating Menkel-Meadow's vision of legal education as a vehicle for broader conflict resolution capabilities and the cultivation of a Human-Centered Lawyer.

title: Waste Minimization Techniques in High-Throughput Printed Electronics Production

detail.title: Waste Minimization Techniques in High-Throughput Printed Electronics Production
detail.abstract: High-throughput printed electronics manufacturing enables large-scale production of flexible and lightweight electronic devices, but it also introduces significant material and process-related waste challenges (Wiklund et al., 2021). Waste generated from excessive ink usage, defective prints, substrate trimming, and inefficient post-processing increases production costs and environmental impact, particularly in roll-to-roll and continuous printing systems (Perelaer et al., 2010). This study examines waste minimization techniques applied across materials, processes, and system-level manufacturing strategies in high-throughput printed electronics production (Pingale and Altay, 2025). A structured synthesis of peer-reviewed literature was conducted to evaluate waste sources and reduction approaches in inkjet, gravure, screen, and roll-to-roll printing technologies (Tiara et al., 2022). The analysis focuses on material utilization efficiency, yield improvement, and scalability of proposed solutions (Kamarudin et al., 2024). Findings indicate that integrated strategies combining optimized ink formulations, precise deposition control, and real-time process monitoring significantly reduce material waste while improving production yield (Islam et al., 2025). Unexpectedly, system-level coordination was found to have a greater impact on waste reduction than isolated material innovations alone (Chavan et al., 2025). The study concludes that waste minimization in high-throughput printed electronics requires a holistic manufacturing approach to support sustainable, scalable, and economically viable industrial production (Pingale and Altay, 2025).

detail.abstract: Workers are increasingly using AI to assist in the performance of work tasks. Although the selfdirected benefits and drawbacks of AI usage have received scholarly attention, less is known about how co-workers react to a focal worker's usage of AI, especially when such worker produces low quality outputs and makes mistakes. Interestingly, the impact of AI usage on the effect of poor performance could go either way: When using AI, one may be perceived either less responsible for the outputs, because part of the work is performed by another agent (i.e., the AI), or more responsible, because AI is known to hallucinate and AI users are expected to ensure that, when they use AI outputs, such outputs are truthful and correct. On a sample of 341 business school students, we tested our hypotheses in a co-working scenario where a colleague (i.e., peer) provided inputs necessary to one's work performance. In support of the latter argument, we found that the negative effect of the peer's poor work quality on peer evaluation by participants was amplified when the peer used AI. We identified perceived responsibility as a mediating mechanism of the moderation. Moreover, we found that more negative affect mediated the moderated effect of low work quality on peer evaluation. Thus, a peer's poor performance has a more negative effect on peer evaluation through an affective mechanism when the peer uses AI, because the peer is deemed more responsible for the work quality. This finding holds important implications for work collaboration under AI usage.

detail.abstract: The EU Court of Justice considers since Altmark that the effects of an aid consisting in the distortion or threat of distortion of competition and effects on trade between Member States are part of the state aid concept, under Article 107(1) of the TFEU. A State that wishes to grant aid will only be subject to the requirement of notification to the European Commission and to the obligation of non-implementation of the aid (pending a Commission decision) provided that the aid fulfils those requirements. Recently, a commentator considered that «the most fundamental defect in the Commission’s State aid practice is that when it finds that a measure is selective, it assumes almost automatically that it distorts competition, although this assumption is not justified». To realize the extent to which such situations may happen it is necessary to determine the exact content of those requirements. That is the object of this paper.

title: Optimization Strategies for Yield Improvement in Roll-to-Roll Manufacturing Systems

detail.title: Optimization Strategies for Yield Improvement in Roll-to-Roll Manufacturing Systems
detail.abstract: This research examines optimization strategies for improving yield in roll-to-roll manufacturing systems, focusing on mechanical design, process monitoring, and system-level control integration (Pingale and Altay 2025). Roll-to-roll manufacturing enables high-throughput production of flexible electronics and energy devices, but persistent yield losses limit scalability and cost efficiency (Potoczny 2023). This study synthesizes prior experimental results, industrial case studies, and system modeling research to identify dominant sources of yield loss and evaluate effective optimization approaches (Martin et al. 2025). Findings indicate that yield degradation is primarily driven by web strain non-uniformity, coating instability, and delayed defect detection (Kang et al. 2020; Maize et al. 2023). Integrated optimization strategies that combine mechanical redesign with real-time metrology and adaptive control demonstrate the highest yield improvements across applications (Pingale and Altay 2025). The study concludes that sustainable yield enhancement requires a coordinated framework that aligns process design, sensing, and control rather than isolated interventions (Daniel et al. 2021).

title: Analysis of the Alignment between Accounting Software Features and the Accounting Cycle Needs of Service and Trading Companies among Introductory Accounting Students

detail.title: Analysis of the Alignment between Accounting Software Features and the Accounting Cycle Needs of Service and Trading Companies among Introductory Accounting Students
detail.abstract: This study examines the alignment between accounting software features and the learning needs of the accounting cycle in Introductory Accounting courses. Using the task-technology fit framework, the research evaluates how software functionalities support students' understanding of transaction recording, summarizing, adjusting, and financial reporting in service and trading company contexts. Data were collected from undergraduate accounting students through questionnaires, observations, and supporting documentation, and analyzed using descriptive statistics and feature-alignment scoring. The findings indicate that accounting software effectively supports learning at the transaction recording and financial reporting stages, particularly in service company accounting cycles. However, misalignment is identified at the summarizing and adjusting stages, especially in trading companies, due to high levels of automation and limited conceptual transparency. These results suggest that while accounting software enhances efficiency and practical exposure, its pedagogical effectiveness depends on instructional integration. The study highlights the importance of aligning software selection, curriculum design, and teaching strategies to ensure meaningful learning outcomes in introductory accounting education.

detail.abstract: We study how the end of the quota system for textiles and clothing products in the American and European markets on January 1, 2005, affected China’s exports to third countries, where policy was unchanged. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that the number of Chinese firms exporting previously restricted products to third countries increased sharply after quota removal. The expansion involved many private firms that exported to neither US-EU markets before nor after 2005. This indicates that the policy shock enhanced China’s role as an export base. Conversely, protectionist shifts in large economies would likely generate sizeable negative third-market effects.

detail.title: Comparison of Manual and Digital Ledgers: Their Impact on Error Detection and Accounting Process Efficiency. RPS Accounting Management Together
detail.abstract: The general ledger plays a central role in the accounting cycle, serving as the foundation for accurate financial reporting. In introductory accounting education, students traditionally learn general ledger procedures through manual recording methods, which support conceptual understanding but often present challenges related to error frequency and time efficiency. Alongside these challenges, the increasing adoption of digital general ledger systems in higher education has transformed how accounting is taught and practiced. This study aims to compare the use of manual and digital general ledgers in terms of students' error detection ability and accounting process efficiency. Using a quantitative comparative quasi-experimental design, the study involves introductory accounting students and employs practical tests, observation sheets, and questionnaires as research instruments. The findings indicate that digital general ledger systems significantly improve accuracy, speed, and error detection, while manual methods remain effective for strengthening foundational accounting concepts. The results imply that a blended instructional approach aligned with the course syllabus (RPS MNJ Bersama) can enhance learning outcomes in introductory accounting education.

detail.abstract: The author, James Ron, reflects on his failure to seriously engage with the Iraq War as a teacher and researcher, He documents his unwillingness to engage, and then offers several hypotheses as to why he did so. He identifies both personal and institutional forces that collectively conspired to push the Iraq War off his teaching and research agenda.

title: Sherlocking: The Effects of Platform-Owner Entry on the Competitive Behavior of Third-Party Firms

detail.title: Sherlocking: The Effects of Platform-Owner Entry on the Competitive Behavior of Third-Party Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: I study how third-party firms respond when a platform owner enters its own marketplace, analyzing Apple's entries into App Store submarkets from 2016-2021. Using text embeddings to define markets and a staggered difference-in-differences design, I find that Apple's entry deters new competitors and shifts incumbents' monetization strategies, but effects vary widely: many markets show no meaningful response, while others move in opposing directions across a host of monetization and quality outcomes. Responses depend on how Apple enters and apps' competitive proximity to Apple. This heterogeneity suggests targeted oversight rather than categorical restrictions on platform-owner entry.
